FIELD REFERENCE

Milkfish (Chanos chanos): habitat, size and identification

Milkfish (Chanos chanos) are silver, toothless fish with a deeply forked tail. Adults form schools in warm coastal waters and around islands. Young fish use mangroves, estuaries and lagoons, and some enter freshwater lakes. Match the scientific name and body features before relying on a local name or choosing a fishing destination.

Updated 2026-11-19 · Castward

Where do milkfish live, and how big do they get?

Key factDetail
Scientific nameChanos chanos
IdentificationSmall toothless mouth, silver body and deeply forked tail — Smithsonian
Adult habitatWarm coastal waters and waters around islands — FAO
Juvenile habitatMangroves, estuaries, coastal lagoons and sometimes freshwater lakes — FAO
Maximum reported length180 cm in the Smithsonian species account; this is not a typical catch size
Eastern Pacific rangeSouthern California to Peru — Smithsonian

What should you know about milkfish?

Are milkfish freshwater or saltwater fish?

They use both. FAO describes coastal adults and young fish in estuaries, mangroves and sometimes freshwater lakes. Spawning takes place in seawater.

Do milkfish have teeth?

The Smithsonian identification account describes a small mouth without teeth. Also check the silver body and deeply forked tail.

How big can milkfish get?

The Smithsonian account lists 180 cm. That maximum does not describe an average fish or promise a catch of that size.

What do milkfish eat?

FAO lists small, soft food items, including microbial mats, detritus, epiphytes and zooplankton. Diet alone does not establish a reliable local fishing method.

Does a country record mean I can fish for milkfish there?

No. A range record establishes occurrence. Confirm access, the exact water and local fishing rules before travel.
